steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every evening, Martin climbed the 127 steps.

He had counted them the first week, thirty years ago, when his knees were young and the lighthouse smelled of fresh paint and possibility. Now the steps smelled of salt and rust and the particular loneliness that settles into iron like a stain.

His wife had lasted two years on the island. He didn't blame her. There was nothing to blame except the sea, and the sea didn't care about blame.

He trimmed the wick with the same deliberate care a surgeon might give to something vital. Outside, November was doing what November does — throwing itself against the rocks, furious and grey. A freighter had gone down on the shoal in 1987, twelve men. Martin had watched the lights disappear one by one from his window. He kept their names on a piece of paper in his coat pocket. He wasn't sure why. Perhaps so someone was carrying them.

The light began its slow rotation.

A supply boat came Tuesdays. The man who drove it, a young fellow named Derek, had mentioned last week that automation was coming. Sensors and satellites. No keeper required.

Martin watched the beam sweep out across the black water, patient and absolute, asking nothing, warning everything.

He supposed the light would keep without him.

He climbed back down. Made tea. Counted the steps anyway — all 127 of them — because some things deserve to be counted.
